slides.alt: A card calls remove_evens([2, 4, 6, 7]) and shows the cells 2, 4, 6, 7; under "returns" are 4 and 7.

slides.text: It's like checking tickets along a row of seats while everyone slides left under your finger.
slides.alt: "Checking tickets, seat by seat": four cinema seats, 0 to 3. A finger points at seat 1, holding 6, while 4 sits in seat 0, ringed, over the line "4 slid into seat 0. Nobody checked it."

slides.text: remove() deletes the value and shifts everything after it one step left, so the next item lands in the slot you just checked, and the loop skips it.
slides.alt: Python remove_evens(nums) with the loop for n in nums: if n % 2 == 0: nums.remove(n) highlighted. The note reads "The next item lands in the slot you just checked: skipped", above cells 4 and 7 and the result "returns [4, 7]: 4 survived".

slides.text: Fix 1: don't edit the list you're reading. Build a new one:
slides.alt: The fix as one line, return [n for n in nums if n % 2 != 0], highlighted. The note reads "Build a new one: keep n only if it's odd", [2, 4, 6, 7] → [7] ✓, with 2, 4 and 6 dimmed and 7 lit: new list: [7].

slides.text: Copy each keeper to write and move write forward. Write never passes read, so nothing unread is overwritten.
slides.alt: The in-place fix: write = 0; for read in range(len(nums)): if nums[read] % 2 != 0: nums[write] = nums[read]; write += 1; then del nums[write:]. The copy line is highlighted. The note reads "write never passes read: nothing unread is overwritten" over cells 7, 4, 6, 7 with write above index 0 and read below index 3: write → 1, never past read.

slides.text: Our test run on 100,000 numbers: 7,972 ms vs 4 ms for the new list.
slides.alt: "100,000 numbers, our test run, Python": every remove shifts the whole tail, O(n²). for n in nums[:]: nums.remove(n) takes 7,972 ms; [n for n in nums if n % 2 != 0] takes 4 ms. A tag says about 2,000× slower.
